[[:db/retract 17592186180087 :question/answer-fields 17592186178191] {:db/id 17592186179767 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6cb153c3-10ae-52e4-a409-49d1a1150376"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179428 :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v+7 \\ u+v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $\mathbf T$ maps the endpoints of $\overline{PQ}$ to the endpoints of $\overline{P'Q'}.$ So, to find the image of $\overline{PQ},$ we find the images of each endpoint.

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing the endpoints of our segment:
![](images/8c/8c18a13c717349bccc5af673ee81a9cdc56f9f2a5c32ce75dc8e63fe91765b1e.svg)

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $\mathbf b$ in each column:
![](images/16/16c730f4e70bed4d3c8bd9840b457a3cfdad3905b0ada078e71044b73f3f2800.svg)

The image of $\mathbf u$ under $\mathbf T$ is given by $A\mathbf u + \mathbf b.$ So, by applying $\mathbf T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-5 & -5 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7 & 7 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-7 & -10 \\ -3 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}7 & 7 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -3 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the endpoints of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(0,-2)$ and $(-3,1).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](images/61/61508357c514f50b27498bee50dce36d22b7f55f0baf8c2d6a58ad2d53dc879d.png)" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179429 :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v+1 \\ u+v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $\mathbf T$ maps the boundary of $\Delta$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $\Delta,$ we find the images of each side.

![](images/69/69d92e24d5b0c81e54d3878793efe7c07d16fc963222997fe4fec4ffb3f93bd5.png)

          

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our square:
![](images/18/1811ded1ce67ec4ebb443816fdf3eb0080b84c6f84852a04b9b66b4e3df35de6.svg)

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $\mathbf b$ in each column:
![](images/11/1110f6582a0a398accdf5a7cda1cd9676e79ecc251fa5ef2c080fc19867e0096.svg)

The image of $\mathbf u$ under $T$ is given by $A\mathbf u + \mathbf b.$ So, by applying $\mathbf T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertices of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(1,-2), (3,0), (1,2),$ and $(-1,0).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](images/dd/ddd14bdebe21c830396e044721811cf6b9c7bd7db067e4d0ff7d35e02a592894.png)

          

Notice that since $\det(A) = 2 >    0,$ this transformation is orientation-preserving." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179430 :question/problem "Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ defined as

$$
x = v - u-6, \qquad y = v -2u  .
$$

Let $A$ be the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- ![](images/13/135271f9b5fd7e9883b49d02ab2abcb2ed268081e887892e5c251c27de1e85de.svg)

- $\det(A) = 1$

- The transformation $\mathbf T$ is orientation-preserving" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}v-u-6 \\ v-2u\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-u+v \\ -2u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T$ is ![](images/dc/dc6ad7fdd5273aa2af71efc5963804edb118fee37596c36a6be3bd30b62467cc.svg)

- Statement II is true. Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get
![](images/42/4266dd2d8188293cb54af9bd8431e27b5ec6e5d936f56363fd692b20b0735e74.svg)

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $\det(A) > 0,$ the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is orientation-preserving.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179773 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-914af94d-7042-54e6-acb1-fed694c9a4de"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179434 :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u+4 \\ 4v-2u\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u \\ -2u+4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T$ is ![](images/78/783a9503543c1305d982dd65a5f3929398f51db97442606bc03f96484aa03e58.svg)

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get
![](images/75/7582ffa6b92e0cba1d8e303231754cfa98a30cfe242d7a6744442462102a02ed.svg)

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is

$$
|\det(A)| = |12| =12.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-6cb153c3-10ae-52e4-a409-49d1a1150376" :question/id #uuid "6cb153c3-10ae-52e4-a409-49d1a1150376" :question/math-academy-id "q-124153" :question/problem "Consider the transformation $T$ defined as

$$
x=4u+v-1,\,y=-u-3v+1.
$$

Let $P(-3,1)$ be a point in the $uv$-plane. Suppose that the image of $P$ under the action of $T$ is the point ${P}^{′}$ in the $xy$-plane. What are the coordinates of ${P}^{′}?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4u+v-1 \\ -u-3v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4u+v \\ -u-3v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the image of $P$ under the action of $T,$ we first create a column vector $u$ containing the coordinates of $P:$ 

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Applying $T$ to $u,$ we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-12 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the coordinates of ${P}^{′}$ are $(-12,1).$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-69877276-8edf-5389-b9b6-59ddab5b630a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-69877276-8edf-5389-b9b6-59ddab5b630a" :answer-field/id #uuid "69877276-8edf-5389-b9b6-59ddab5b630a" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-79732bdc-fd7e-5901-92b4-c5585d62e3b9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-15292884-dc42-57e9-9c54-15240ddfccc9" "answer-99809079-4b95-5960-860d-5696a69fc28e" "answer-73315599-47f7-5acb-b194-b9be8f07b4fe" "answer-79732bdc-fd7e-5901-92b4-c5585d62e3b9" "answer-94a311b2-4197-58fb-9f74-f9df05de251a"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-15292884-dc42-57e9-9c54-15240ddfccc9" :answer/id #uuid "15292884-dc42-57e9-9c54-15240ddfccc9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-1,12)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-99809079-4b95-5960-860d-5696a69fc28e" :answer/id #uuid "99809079-4b95-5960-860d-5696a69fc28e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-11,-1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-73315599-47f7-5acb-b194-b9be8f07b4fe" :answer/id #uuid "73315599-47f7-5acb-b194-b9be8f07b4fe" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-11,0)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-79732bdc-fd7e-5901-92b4-c5585d62e3b9" :answer/id #uuid "79732bdc-fd7e-5901-92b4-c5585d62e3b9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(-12,1)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-94a311b2-4197-58fb-9f74-f9df05de251a" :answer/id #uuid "94a311b2-4197-58fb-9f74-f9df05de251a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "(1,12)" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-914af94d-7042-54e6-acb1-fed694c9a4de" :question/id #uuid "914af94d-7042-54e6-acb1-fed694c9a4de" :question/math-academy-id "q-162181" :question/problem "Consider the affine transformation $T,$ defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

What is the area scale factor of the transformation?" :question/worked-solution "The matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}].$ 

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}|=1\cdot 4-3\cdot 2=-2.
$$

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is

$$
|det(A)|=|-2|=2.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-cc6bf158-bc5a-5b83-aecb-e172b7a9b66e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-cc6bf158-bc5a-5b83-aecb-e172b7a9b66e" :answer-field/id #uuid "cc6bf158-bc5a-5b83-aecb-e172b7a9b66e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-76b47f26-b551-5ab2-a16b-a5772ef735ad" :answer-field/choices ["answer-f0b0cc75-4660-5f89-b375-205d3cc92d47" "answer-d2847d2c-57b6-59e8-b9ce-cd6f7d5c8fab" "answer-76b47f26-b551-5ab2-a16b-a5772ef735ad" "answer-0bc4fab2-f286-5943-a45f-a20492b01ffd" "answer-ca24dbee-3bf2-5067-b768-9753b1ef80ef"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-f0b0cc75-4660-5f89-b375-205d3cc92d47" :answer/id #uuid "f0b0cc75-4660-5f89-b375-205d3cc92d47" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d2847d2c-57b6-59e8-b9ce-cd6f7d5c8fab" :answer/id #uuid "d2847d2c-57b6-59e8-b9ce-cd6f7d5c8fab" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-76b47f26-b551-5ab2-a16b-a5772ef735ad" :answer/id #uuid "76b47f26-b551-5ab2-a16b-a5772ef735ad" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0bc4fab2-f286-5943-a45f-a20492b01ffd" :answer/id #uuid "0bc4fab2-f286-5943-a45f-a20492b01ffd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "4" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ca24dbee-3bf2-5067-b768-9753b1ef80ef" :answer/id #uuid "ca24dbee-3bf2-5067-b768-9753b1ef80ef" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "6" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180755 :tutorial/content "Consider the triangle $\Delta$ with sides $S_1, S_2,$ and $S_3,$  shown below. Let's imagine that we traverse the boundary once in the counterclockwise direction starting from the origin.

![](images/23/231dd5f96cd36d21940fcee894382edc9eabc91b0bf72bb4a8724c8444f76a8c.png)

Let the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ be defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T,$ we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our triangle, presented in the order shown in the diagram:
![](images/34/34be6d7cd24938fb72976910cf3ad6a790eb93574915829f621da99f4aec3838.svg)

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $\mathbf b$ in each column:
![](images/be/bed30fcc6a1003bee7f2f7888af9c301314b2aba351497db35cf2ee37710c0a1.svg)

The image of $\mathbf u$ under $T$ is given by $A\mathbf u + \mathbf b.$ So, by applying $\mathbf T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The vertices of the image are given by the columns of the above matrix. Drawing these vertices in the order shown, i.e.

$$
(1,-1) \to (1,0) \to (2,-1),
$$

we get the following picture:

![](images/d5/d514834e6e9f108f478002416e863cf9c98d00add230c2e9321664ea14e5db0e.png)

          

Notice that the polygon $D$ is traversed in the *clockwise* direction." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180756 :tutorial/content "An invertible affine transformation is **orientation-preserving** if it preserves the orientation of any polygon in the plane.

To understand this, let's go back to our triangle $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane and its image $D$ in the $xy$-plane under the action of the affine transformation $\mathbf T.$ 

![](images/b5/b5c33feb218ae0c1c32aa61984d01b5a317ab88f78277e01c20111a2c0c4efe5.png)

This transformation does *not* preserve orientation because when we traverse $\Delta$ *counterclockwise*, its image $D$ is traversed *clockwise.*

We can identify whether an affine transformation is orientation-preserving or not by examining the matrix $A$ of the associated linear map. We have the following theorem:

*Suppose an affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is defined as* 

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

*where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. Then, $\mathbf{T}$ preserves orientation if*

$$
\det(A) > 0,
$$

*and does not preserve orientation if*

$$
\det(A) < 0.
$$

We sometimes refer to cases where $\det(A) < 0$ as **orientation-reversing.**" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180760 :tutorial/content "Suppose an affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$  is defined as

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Similar to the case of linear transformations, the ** area scale factor** of $\mathbf T$ is given by the determinant of $A.$

We can identify whether an affine transformation increases or decreases the area of a polygon $\mathcal P$ by examining the area scale factor:

- If $|\det(A)|>1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *larger* area than $\mathcal P.$

- If $|\det(A)|=1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have the *same* area as $\mathcal P.$

- If $0 < |\det(A)| < 1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *smaller* area than $\mathcal P.$

Note that if $\det(A) = 0,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ is not a polygon. We discuss this case in more detail in a separate lesson.

For example, consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2,$ from the previous discussion, defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get
![](images/7c/7c637211f31b2e8e49fb56f6e60573c47bada4fa36b6c6e0fa7474c3e4d106fc.svg)

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is

$$
|\det(A)| = |-1| = 1.
$$

Thus, the area of triangle $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane and its image $D$ under $\mathbf T$ in the $xy$-plane have the same area. 

![](images/b5/b5c33feb218ae0c1c32aa61984d01b5a317ab88f78277e01c20111a2c0c4efe5.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179859 :activity/expected-seconds 960.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}]

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Notice that since $\det(A) = 2 >    0,$ this transformation is orientation-preserving." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179430 :question/problem "Consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ defined as

- $\det(A) = 1$

- The transformation $\mathbf T$ is orientation-preserving" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}v-u-6 \\ v-2u\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-u+v \\ -2u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $\det(A) > 0,$ the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ is orientation-preserving.

Let $P(-3,1)$ be a point in the $uv$-plane. Suppose that the image of $P$ under the action of $T$ is the point ${P}^{′}$ in the $xy$-plane. What are the coordinates of ${P}^{′}?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4u+v-1 \\ -u-3v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4u+v \\ -u-3v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ -1 & -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}

$$

$$

The image of $\mathbf u$ under $T$ is given by $A\mathbf u + \mathbf b.$ So, by applying $\mathbf T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

![](images/d5/d514834e6e9f108f478002416e863cf9c98d00add230c2e9321664ea14e5db0e.png)

          

Notice that the polygon $D$ is traversed in the *clockwise* direction." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180756 :tutorial/content "An invertible affine transformation is **orientation-preserving** if it preserves the orientation of any polygon in the plane.

To understand this, let's go back to our triangle $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane and its image $D$ in the $xy$-plane under the action of the affine transformation $\mathbf T.$ 

![](images/b5/b5c33feb218ae0c1c32aa61984d01b5a317ab88f78277e01c20111a2c0c4efe5.png)

This transformation does *not* preserve orientation because when we traverse $\Delta$ *counterclockwise*, its image $D$ is traversed *clockwise.*

We can identify whether an affine transformation is orientation-preserving or not by examining the matrix $A$ of the associated linear map. We have the following theorem:

*Suppose an affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is defined as* 

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

*where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. Then, $\mathbf{T}$ preserves orientation if*

$$
\det(A) > 0,
$$

*and does not preserve orientation if*

$$
\det(A) < 0.
$$

We sometimes refer to cases where $\det(A) < 0$ as **orientation-reversing.**" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180760 :tutorial/content "Suppose an affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$  is defined as

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Similar to the case of linear transformations, the ** area scale factor** of $\mathbf T$ is given by the determinant of $A.$

We can identify whether an affine transformation increases or decreases the area of a polygon $\mathcal P$ by examining the area scale factor:

- If $|\det(A)|>1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *larger* area than $\mathcal P.$

- If $|\det(A)|=1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have the *same* area as $\mathcal P.$

- If $0 < |\det(A)| < 1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *smaller* area than $\mathcal P.$

Note that if $\det(A) = 0,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ is not a polygon. We discuss this case in more detail in a separate lesson.

For example, consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2,$ from the previous discussion, defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is

$$

$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Similar to the case of linear transformations, the ** area scale factor** of $\mathbf T$ is given by the determinant of $A.$

We can identify whether an affine transformation increases or decreases the area of a polygon $\mathcal P$ by examining the area scale factor:

- If $|\det(A)|>1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *larger* area than $\mathcal P.$

- If $|\det(A)|=1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have the *same* area as $\mathcal P.$

- If $0 < |\det(A)| < 1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *smaller* area than $\mathcal P.$

Note that if $\det(A) = 0,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ is not a polygon. We discuss this case in more detail in a separate lesson.

For example, consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2,$ from the previous discussion, defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is

$$
|\det(A)| = |-1| = 1.
$$

We can identify whether an affine transformation is orientation-preserving or not by examining the matrix $A$ of the associated linear map. We have the following theorem:

*Suppose an affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is defined as* $$\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$ *where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. Similar to the case of linear transformations, the **area scale factor** of $\mathbf T$ is given by the determinant of $A.$

We can identify whether an affine transformation increases or decreases the area of a polygon $\mathcal P$ by examining the area scale factor:

- If $|\det(A)|>1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *larger* area than $\mathcal P.$
- If $|\det(A)|=1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have the *same* area as $\mathcal P.$
- If $0 < |\det(A)| < 1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *smaller* area than $\mathcal P.$

Note that if $\det(A) = 0,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ is not a polygon. We discuss this case in more detail in a separate lesson.

For example, consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2,$ from the previous discussion, defined as

$$\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get $$\det(A) = \left| \begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned} \right| = 0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1 =-1.$$

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is $$|\det(A)| = |-1| = 1.$$

Thus, the area of triangle $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane and its image $D$ under $\mathbf T$ in the $xy$-plane have the same area.

$$

$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u+v-2 \\ u-2v+1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u+v \\ u-2v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the image of $P$ under the action of $T,$ we first create a column vector $u$ containing the coordinates of $P:$

$$
u=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Applying $T$ to $u,$ we get

$$
[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Affine Transformation"}] :question/problem "![](images/dd/dd8b1407add93e72afccf2138cc818df63d47fdaa6ccc23e843a5602d8c1dbd8.png)

          

Consider the rectangle $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane, given by

$$
\Delta  = \big\{ (u,v) \: : \: -1 \leq u \leq 1, \: -1\leq v \leq 1 \big\}.
$$

The transformation $\mathbf T$ is defined as

$$
x = u - v + 1, \qquad y = u+v
$$

Find the image of $\Delta$ in the $xy$-plane under the action of $\mathbf T.$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as 

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}u-v+1 \\ u+v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u-v \\ u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $\mathbf T$ maps the boundary of $\Delta$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $\Delta,$ we find the images of each side.

![](images/69/69d92e24d5b0c81e54d3878793efe7c07d16fc963222997fe4fec4ffb3f93bd5.png)

          

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our square:
![](images/04/047cd6bf2960418919b4a11ae6920d9fc589881062ddbb3eed918116a7e4c4fd.png)

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $\mathbf b$ in each column:
![](images/cf/cfc1c3e72dd7764d9835e35f1943ef96c6829703ca8f0b2bce67153df9df88e5.png)

The image of $\mathbf u$ under $T$ is given by $A\mathbf u + \mathbf b.$ So, by applying $\mathbf T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -1 & -1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 0 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertices of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(1,-2), (3,0), (1,2),$ and $(-1,0).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following:

![](images/dd/ddd14bdebe21c830396e044721811cf6b9c7bd7db067e4d0ff7d35e02a592894.png)

          

Notice that since $\det(A) = 2 >    0,$ this transformation is orientation-preserving."} {:db/id 17592186179987 :question/id #uuid "e82788c7-cc00-5020-bbcf-2ea37a04c3e9" :question/math-academy-id $$
Δ={(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 2,\,0\le v\le 1}.
$$

The transformation $T$ is defined as

$$

$$

Which of the following gives the image of $Δ$ in the $xy$-plane under the action of $T?$" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that we can express the given transformation as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1-u \\ 2-v\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-u \\ -v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

The transformation $T$ maps the boundary of $Δ$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $Δ,$ we find the images of each side.

![](images/a8/a8a13c579c3ca8cc32f997c48e237c38d449aa07040de658589fa5cc68a02c55.png)

          

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our square:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $b$ in each column:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

The image of $u$ under $T$ is given by $Au+b.$ So, by applying $T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertices of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(2,2),(-1,2),(-1,1),$ and $(2,1).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following: 

![](images/14/146f9f36deeac0f3a7108a173485eb6d0d03138d18998a96dc9c3566bee21ca2.png)

          

Finally, since $det(A)=1>0,$ this transformation is orientation-preserving."} {:db/id 17592186259690 :question/id #uuid "6fdc3f93-8486-56f6-8744-50fa49ca621b" :question/math-academy-id "q-124561" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "75895875-a73e-5cbb-bf3d-c5aa2a0d474a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/d1/d1e93d9ce18d7c75ab6432d53ae9ff72fd3fe2c89125a12dcd2d41a13100465d.png" :db/id 17592186257813} {:answer/id #uuid "7e96b286-9f53-5a16-a78e-11d14b7729bf" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/82/8254c51a8f1c9f0ca48f169fb48a938b07e5812b5be866d9ab25e5fbdffed368.png" :db/id 17592186257908} {:answer/id #uuid "8db86e0e-3c7f-5fc7-8dd6-cb016f66e98b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/6b/6be30b91e0526e28530b4c5cfff6c0c5e7be53a77e587c5eb37a845b6cc0a189.png" :db/id 17592186258028} {:answer/id #uuid "aac5b30f-88de-5a6d-a659-c1f1d57058a8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/a7/a7b171394aeccd9b807fc29ecf7c33f745c58bce3ed01bcf879a79d2edf97319.png" :db/id 17592186258271} {:answer/id #uuid "c68d0b11-70cb-55fa-8c98-86952dd0839e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045497} :answer/value "images/27/27dbdbec3125bdef5109bf6aa549c9bcfe83175b42e660cc44977540de0ad112.png" :db/id 17592186258517}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186257813} :answer-field/id #uuid "047ad574-9503-5413-9fac-632c989f1e97" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259040}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "![](images/79/79b09bcf02998adf6d7bf19e7d59cabdc563ff26266966440bbb49be53029ac3.png)

![](images/06/06ceacb05656e99e545561e5cd5733529a1cf7f052beb6086b2fd42667041713.png)

          

To quickly carry out this calculation, we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our square:

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $b$ in each column:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

The image of $u$ under $T$ is given by $Au+b.$ So, by applying $T$ to $U,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ -2 & 0 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertices of the image in the $xy$-plane are $(-1,-2),(1,0),(2,-1),$ and $(0,-3).$

Drawing this region in the $xy$-plane, we get the following: 

![](images/92/92b9079151925202a5346e6b1dd2082b21a4e4102720673773e958c5f3644c4f.png)

          

Finally, since $det(A)=-2<0,$ this transformation is not orientation-preserving."} {:db/id 17592186387505 :question/id #uuid "b8c4a4f3-ae6f-5810-a76c-6ebd19065fd9" :question/math-academy-id What is the area scale factor of the transformation?" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form

$$
\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,
$$

where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3u+4 \\ 4v-2u\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3u \\ -2u+4v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $\mathbf T$ is ![](images/8c/8c90983944994c315715ff8545d3cffd5e791c23e8ad035bdc3b4c810659442e.png)

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get
![](images/a9/a9a49eaf4203133b1c47ab30b75fde67af56172ae6c4e59d12a2f7e9df3d46c1.png)

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is

$$
|\det(A)| = |12| =12.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186049339} {:db/id 17592186180086 :question/id #uuid "23554130-d2fa-542b-a17b-f4f9de21608d" :question/math-academy-id "q-162141"} {:db/id 17592186180087 :question/id #uuid What is the area scale factor of the transformation?" :question/worked-solution "The matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}|=3\cdot 1-(-1)\cdot (-1)=2.
$$

$$
|det(A)|=|2|=2.

[{:db/id 17592186180553 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180754 :tutorial/content "To find the image of a point under an affine transformation, all we need to do is substitute the position vector of the point into the formula for the affine transformation.

For example, consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\Bbb R^2 \to \Bbb R^2,$ defined by

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Suppose that the point $P({\color{black}-1},{\color{black}1})$ with position vector $\mathbf p$ lies in the $uv$-plane, as shown below. 

![](images/06/06c9283bde54e329d31d5892702e4a75c0ca78bd21ee3bb23f9a2b748239bf14.png)

We can find the image of $P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ by substituting $\mathbf p$ into the affine transformation formula: 

$$
\begin{aligned}T(P) & =Ap+b \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the image of $P$ is the point $P'({\color{black}-1},{\color{black}3})$ in the $xy$-plane.

We can visualize $P$ and its image under $\mathbf T$ using a diagram like the one below.

![](images/89/893933990225c54e0a3327de70f29b3d73af2b829cf53053d155bb52d5202e63.png)

We can use a similar method to map multiple points from the $uv$-plane to the $xy$-plane using just one calculation. Let's see how." :tutorial/id #uuid "b71d5e38-7267-5428-89f5-941492316127" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7694 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "7e42cdff-0162-5f00-9062-0bbf4e7ef4c8" :step/math-academy-id 44648 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180554}} {:db/id 17592186180554 :step/content {:db/id 17592186179767 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186179428 :question/id #uuid "102d79a9-f19c-5735-a3f2-347938820b19" :question/math-academy-id "e-12425"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "8ba09dd1-d219-5df2-adfa-d88d7b9fc481" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186049012} {:db/id 17592186049420}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186179989} {:db/id 17592186179991} {:db/id 17592186259598} {:db/id 17592186259599} {:db/id 17592186259600} {:db/id 17592186259607} {:db/id 17592186371693} {:db/id 17592186387463}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding the Image of a Point or Segment"} :step/id #uuid "130575e3-c9fd-5688-a557-9be7454f3b61" :step/math-academy-id 44649 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180555}} {:db/id 17592186180555 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180755 :tutorial/content "Consider the triangle $\Delta$ with sides $S_1, S_2,$ and $S_3,$ shown below. Let's imagine that we traverse the boundary once in the counterclockwise direction starting from the origin.

![](images/23/231dd5f96cd36d21940fcee894382edc9eabc91b0bf72bb4a8724c8444f76a8c.png)

Let the affine transformation $\mathbf T$ be defined as

$$\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}$$

To find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T,$ we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our triangle, presented in the order shown in the diagram: $$U = [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$$
- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $\mathbf b$ in each column: $$B = [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]$$

The image of $\mathbf u$ under $T$ is given by $A\mathbf u + \mathbf b.$ So, by applying $\mathbf T$ to $U,$ we get

$$\begin{aligned}AU+B & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\ & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ -1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}$$

The vertices of the image are given by the columns of the above matrix. Drawing these vertices in the order shown, i.e.

$$(1,-1) \to (1,0) \to (2,-1),$$

we get the following picture:

![](images/d5/d514834e6e9f108f478002416e863cf9c98d00add230c2e9321664ea14e5db0e.png)

Notice that the polygon $D$ is traversed in the *clockwise* direction." :tutorial/id #uuid "c717442d-1c85-597b-bfc9-3bacde35a1f0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7695 :tutorial/title "Finding the Image of a Polygon"} :step/id #uuid "804e3ae7-0f27-5ff7-9101-bf7c7b3dfa01" :step/math-academy-id 44652 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180556}} {:db/id 17592186180556 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180756 :tutorial/content "An invertible affine transformation is **orientation-preserving** if it preserves the orientation of any polygon in the plane.

To understand this, let's go back to our triangle $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane and its image $D$ in the $xy$-plane under the action of the affine transformation $\mathbf T.$

![](images/b5/b5c33feb218ae0c1c32aa61984d01b5a317ab88f78277e01c20111a2c0c4efe5.png)

This transformation does *not* preserve orientation because when we traverse $\Delta$ *counterclockwise*, its image $D$ is traversed *clockwise.*

We can identify whether an affine transformation is orientation-preserving or not by examining the matrix $A$ of the associated linear map. We have the following theorem:

*Suppose an affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is defined as* $$\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$ *where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix. Then, $\mathbf{T}$ preserves orientation if* $$\det(A) > 0,$$ *and does not preserve orientation if* $$\det(A) < 0.$$

We sometimes refer to cases where $\det(A) < 0$ as **orientation-reversing.**" :tutorial/id #uuid "0444feba-dbdb-5165-942a-79da29a810e0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 7696 :tutorial/title 17592186180567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180760 :tutorial/content "Suppose an affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is defined as $$\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$ where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Similar to the case of linear transformations, the **area scale factor** of $\mathbf T$ is given by the determinant of $A.$

We can identify whether an affine transformation increases or decreases the area of a polygon $\mathcal P$ by examining the area scale factor:

- If $|\det(A)|>1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *larger* area than $\mathcal P.$
- If $|\det(A)|=1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have the *same* area as $\mathcal P.$
- If $0 < |\det(A)| < 1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *smaller* area than $\mathcal P.$

Note that if $\det(A) = 0,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ is not a polygon. We discuss this case in more detail in a separate lesson.

For example, consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2,$ from the previous discussion, defined as

$$\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get $$\det(A) = \left| \begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned} \right| = 0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1 =-1.$$

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is $$|\det(A)| = |-1| = 1.$$

Thus, the area of triangle $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane and its image $D$ under $\mathbf T$ in the $xy$-plane have the same area.

To find the image of $\Delta$ under the action of $\mathbf T,$ we set up the following matrices:

- The matrix $U$ containing all vertices of our triangle, presented in the order shown in the diagram: $$U = [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$$
- The matrix $B$ that has the same shape as $U$ and with the vector $\mathbf b$ in each column: $$B = [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]$$

The image of $\mathbf u$ under $T$ is given by $A\mathbf u + \mathbf b.$ So, by applying $\mathbf T$ to $U,$ we get

The vertices of the image are given by the columns of the above matrix. Drawing these vertices in the order shown, i.e.

$$(1,-1) \to (1,0) \to (2,-1),$$

we get the following picture:

:step/math-academy-id 44657 :step/next {:db/id 17592186180567}} {:db/id 17592186180567 :step/content {:db/id 17592186180760 :tutorial/content "Suppose an affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is defined as $$\mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b,$$ where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Similar to the case of linear transformations, the **area scale factor** of $\mathbf T$ is given by the determinant of $A.$

We can identify whether an affine transformation increases or decreases the area of a polygon $\mathcal P$ by examining the area scale factor:

- If $|\det(A)|>1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *larger* area than $\mathcal P.$
- If $|\det(A)|=1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have the *same* area as $\mathcal P.$
- If $0 < |\det(A)| < 1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *smaller* area than $\mathcal P.$

Note that if $\det(A) = 0,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ is not a polygon. We discuss this case in more detail in a separate lesson.

For example, consider the affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2,$ from the previous discussion, defined as

$$\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}.\end{aligned}$$

Computing the determinant of $A,$ we get $$\det(A) = \left| \begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned} \right| = 0 \cdot 0 - 1 \cdot 1 =-1.$$

So, the area scale factor of the transformation is $$|\det(A)| = |-1| = 1.$$

Thus, the area of triangle $\Delta$ in the $uv$-plane and its image $D$ under $\mathbf T$ in the $xy$-plane have the same area.

$$
x=2v-u+2,\,y=2u+v-5.
$$

Let $A$ be the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]$
- $det(A)=-5$
- The transformation $T$ is orientation-preserving" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. Indeed, notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2v-u+2 \\ 2u+v-5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-u+2v \\ 2u+v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}|=(-1)\cdot 1-2\cdot 2=-5.
$$

- Statement III is false. Since $det(A)<0,$ the affine transformation $T$ is not orientation-preserving.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only.""} :step/id #uuid "0a78ca60-8278-5f69-a0c5-4853a7109868" :step/next {:db/id 17592186408042}} {:db/id 17592186408041 :step/content {:db/id 17592186259616 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0ccab3c0-0254-5090-9c86-829a851b15b0" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I and III only" :db/id 17592186256907} {:answer/id #uuid "2c4c2cb2-f173-5288-817b-371883d27529" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "I only" :db/id 17592186257179} {:answer/id #uuid "60740839-3d41-5df6-8849-4084e44e6ec1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "III only" :db/id 17592186257630} {:answer/id #uuid "b74a87c3-7a0f-5446-af5b-58a1007116ff" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II only" :db/id 17592186258382} {:answer/id #uuid "d661a75a-735f-5ece-a15b-6a8a834246d2" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "II and III only" :db/id 17592186258665}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186258382} :answer-field/id #uuid "33b4cd81-c3a3-52e0-a0d4-355e8ea3aed5" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186259128}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "d0a1ba57-9eac-5d49-9cdd-f7f25fec8c92" :question/math-academy-id "q-124192" :question/problem "Consider the affine transformation $T$ defined as

$$
x=2v+u+1,\,y=u-v-2.
$$

Let $A$ be the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T.$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]$
- $det(A)=-3$
- The transformation $T$ is orientation-preserving" :question/worked-solution "An affine transformation $T:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2}$ is a function of the form

$$
x=Au+b,
$$

where $x,u,$ and $b$ are column vectors in ${R}^{2},$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

Let's look at each statement in turn:

- Statement I is false. Notice that the given transformation can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2v+u+1 \\ u-v-2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}u+2v \\ u-v\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{u}+{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the matrix representation of the linear transformation associated with $T$ is $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, computing the determinant of $A,$ we get

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|=1\cdot (-1)-2\cdot 1=-3.

$$

The transformation $T$ maps the boundary of $Δ$ to the boundary of the image. So, to find the image of $Δ,$ we find the images of each side.

The linear algebra section covers crucial machine learning fundamentals such as matrices, vector spaces, diagonalization, projections, singular value decomposition, and regression, as well as dimensionality reduction techniques such as principal component analysis. The multivariable calculus section develops the tools needed for optimization and learning algorithms, including vector and matrix calculus. Finally, the probability and statistics section covers random variables, point estimation, maximum likelihood estimation, and confidence intervals.

Students then explore matrices in-depth. They study Gaussian elimination, solve systems of equations, learn about determinants and their properties, and compute inverse matrices. These tools form the computational backbone of many machine learning algorithms.
As part of this course, students perform a deep dive into vector spaces, exploring linear independence, subspaces, bases, dimension, rank, and nullity. They also study operations such as the Hadamard product, which appears naturally in element-wise computations in neural networks. Students generalize key concepts to abstract vector spaces and inner product spaces, and study orthogonality, projections, and the Gram–Schmidt process.
Students will learn how to find eigenvectors of a matrix, compute matrix diagonalizations, and extend these ideas to orthogonal diagonalization of symmetric matrices. These techniques underpin dimensionality reduction methods and are central to understanding the structure of data.
The course then develops key applications of linear algebra in machine learning. Students study singular value decomposition and its relationship to principal component analysis, and learn how these tools are used for dimensionality reduction, feature extraction, and identifying structure in high-dimensional datasets. Linear least-squares problems and regression techniques are also studied as foundational methods for fitting models to data.
A solid grasp of multivariable calculus is essential for understanding modern machine learning algorithms. In this course, students become well-versed in partial derivatives and gradient vectors (used in gradient-based optimization), the multivariable chain rule (essential for backpropagation), and vector-valued functions. Students extend differentiation to maps between multi-dimensional vector spaces and develop the tools of vector and matrix calculus used to compute gradients of loss functions in neural networks.
Students also study optimization of multivariable functions, including critical points, second derivative tests, and constrained optimization using Lagrange multipliers. These techniques form the mathematical foundation of algorithms such as support vector machines and constrained optimization problems in machine learning.
Students work with standard multivariable surfaces to build intuition for loss surfaces, and study double integrals as a tool for understanding continuous probability distributions.
On the probability and statistics side, students study discrete and continuous random variables, including probability density functions, cumulative distribution functions, transformations, expectation, moments, variance, and Bayes' theorem. Important probability distributions are explored in detail.
Students extend their understanding to joint, marginal, and conditional distributions, as well as sums and products of random variables. Topics such as covariance, correlation, and multivariate normal distributions are introduced, which are essential in probabilistic modeling.

These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. $$

- If $|\det(A)|=1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have the *same* area as $\mathcal P.$
- If $0 < |\det(A)| < 1,$ the image of $\mathcal P$ under the action of $\mathbf T$ will have a *smaller* area than $\mathcal P.$
